analysis.one_liner: Bans forced arbitration clauses for servicemembers in disputes under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Veterans' Affairs Committee on August 1, 2023, sent to a subcommittee three weeks later, and never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsor before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Military service often overlaps with contracts like car loans, credit cards, leases, and mortgages. The Servicemembers Civil Relief Act gives active-duty troops special legal protections — capped interest, protection from repossession and default judgments — but companies commonly write contracts requiring any dispute to go to a private arbitrator instead of court. This bill would have made those clauses unenforceable for disputes covered by the act: arbitration could happen only if everyone agreed in writing after the dispute arose, companies could only waive servicemembers' rights in a narrow, dispute-specific way, and servicemembers could still sue in court even if a contract said otherwise.
analysis.who_benefits: Active-duty servicemembers and their spouses. When a lender repossesses a car or a creditor exceeds the legal 6% interest cap during deployment, the bill would let the servicemember take the case to a public court with a judge and precedent, instead of a private arbitration process that tends to favor repeat corporate players and can bar class actions.

how_it_helps.text: A contract with a servicemember could require arbitration only if, after the dispute arises, all parties consent in writing — meaning the company could no longer force arbitration through a clause signed at purchase time.
Companies could only waive servicemembers' rights under the act if the waiver is made after a specific dispute has arisen and identifies that dispute, closing the door on broad up-front waivers.
The bill clarifies that servicemembers may sue in court to enforce the act's protections notwithstanding any previous arbitration or waiver agreement.

analysis.who_pays: Consumer lenders, banks, auto finance companies, and the arbitration industry, which would lose the contractual guarantee that disputes with troops stay in arbitration — a forum where companies generally fare better and cannot face class actions. Businesses would also face more lawsuits in court, with higher defense costs in some cases.

drawbacks.text: Arbitration is not always worse for the servicemember: for small-dollar disputes it can be faster and cheaper than court, and a rule letting the business veto arbitration after a dispute arises could push routine claims into more costly litigation.

The bill is narrow: it covers only controversies arising under provisions of the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, not forced arbitration in servicemember contracts generally, so many disputes (such as ordinary breach-of-contract claims outside the act) would still go to arbitration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: enforcing the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act is hard when the contract itself routes every dispute into a private forum, and Congress has already found servicemember legal protections worth protecting by statute. The cost is that businesses lose a predictable, low-cost dispute channel and some small disputes may become more expensive to resolve. On balance the bill would have shifted leverage toward servicemembers in exactly the situations the act was written to protect, with a limited scope that keeps the change narrow.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Veterans' Affairs Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Katie Porter introduced the bill on August 1, 2023.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs, and on August 24, 2023 referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity.
No other action was taken in the House, and the bill received no cosponsors.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill ever leaving committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer lenders, banks, and auto finance companies kept their ability to force disputes with active-duty troops into arbitration, and the arbitration industry kept the business. Servicemembers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Katie Porter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar forced arbitration in Servicemembers Civil Relief Act disputes.

against.name: House Veterans' Affairs Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; after referring it to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, the committee took no further action through the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the partisan shape cannot be measured; the bill was introduced by one Democrat and never advanced in a Republican-controlled committee.

industries.industry: Consumer lenders, banks, and auto finance companies
industries.note: These companies rely on arbitration clauses to keep disputes out of court, where servicemembers can invoke statutory interest caps and repossession protections and where class actions are possible. The bill would have taken that guarantee away for disputes covered by the act. Note: the bill died, so lenders retained the status quo.
Forced-arbitration clauses are these firms' core revenue stream; servicemember contracts covered by the act would no longer have been automatically theirs. The bill's death preserved their business.
